title: Ongoing issues with roofer and I don't know what to do | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hopingforsunshine", "author_name": "hopingforsunshine", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hopingforsunshine", "date": "2023-02-01", "text": "Sorry, a super long-winded ranty, post here, but I've had so much anxiety from day 1 about this and need advice. We've moved to a new area where we don't really know anyone. Our house survey said we had some slipped slates and some flashing/chimney pointing needing doing. We checked out 4 different local roofing companies and asked them to come round to quote. The one we went with had a website, lots of gallery pics of existing work and was on checkatrade. He was the second most expensive but we felt confident he was the right person for the job at the time. After agreeing a price he told me after having already taken down some bits the cost would be more than double agreed as they realised it was all rotten underneath so batons needed to be replaced and they were to add felt. Although horrified at the extra cost, we felt pressure to agree as they'd already started dismantling it and thought \"well if it needs doing, it needs doing\". -The guy who did the \"sell\" to us in the first place and owns the company was nowhere to be found on any of the days except to drop the guys off/drop materials off in the morning and pick them up and check on things when it was already dark in the evening. They definitely had other roofing jobs going on at the same time. - The boys who actually did the work, well I just have a strong feeling they were labourers rather than roofers and it was often different guys on different days. When big mistakes were made the guys the day after would be blaming the guys the day before. - They were hammering new batons on so hard plaster was falling on my head from the ceiling as I worked. - The covering fell off in the night so rain came in and ceilings/walls got wet now there's ugly orange/yellow stains and also long cracks along ceilings and corners of walls in numerous rooms, water marks around electrics like light fittings/switches etc. - Due to another separate error they made, we had a lot of water coming down our bathroom wall and to the floor below so our kitchen wall and bathroom wall is particularly stained. - I had to keep reminding the main guy things hadn't been done yet when he insisted they had, by taking photos and whatsapping actual evidence until he finally got someone to sort it. -Mess everywhere after they left . Slate all over my back yard, old pipes left hidden behind my garage and someone even left half eaten Greggs food and drink there, the temp plastic sheet was also shoved in my garden shed. Since they left, I quickly found a new damp patch on my bathroom ceiling and the external wall that wasn't there when the last lot of leaks happened so I'm really worried something else hasn't been done properly. BUT my roofer has been very evasive, not coming round to fix, stating personal issues and being in hospital. I have asked repeatedly over the past 3 weeks over text (and call but he doesn't often answer), can someone else come and look at this, it doesn't have to be him personally if he's in hospital obviously, but I don't want my house in even worse condition and potentially more serious things happening, but he keeps fobbing me off over text saying no one is looking after his company whilst he's off but he'll try and get someone to sort it soon and his personal problems are his priority right now. I don't want to be a d*ck if he's going through something serious but after this nightmare experience I just feel like it might be another lie and I'm being messed around again. I haven't the funds to get someone else in to fix this as we paid so much money to him in the first place. What do you think I should do? Please help!", "images": []}

title: Garden Design ideas - please help! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-470493970", "author_name": "HU-470493970", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-470493970", "date": "2023-02-01", "text": "I would greatly appreciate any ideas for how to design my garden. As you can see it is pretty much a blank canvas. I have spent many hours trawling the internet for ideas and know that I need to divide the garden into 'rooms' and create a journey down the garden. However I am unsure how to do this. I do have an issue to consider and that is that the previous owner installed the sewage treatment system in the middle of the garden (the green rectangular and 2 circular covers) so that limits what I can plant in that area and therefore how I can screen off/divide the garden. I am unsure if I can plant a hedge as the roots may damage the pipes/tank. I can't plant trees nearby as they may also cause damage. I could put up a trellis screen but not sure I like that idea - I think it may look odd having trellis right in the middle of the garden.If I plant up a bed in front of the tank, it will still be visible from the other side. The far end of the garden has young fruit trees and we have seeded it to be a wildflower meadow so that section is sorted.The greenhouse is going to go as it is terrible condition and an eyesore! I like a natural planting style - lots of grasses, lavender, verbena and would really love to plant more trees but keep coming back to the worry about planting near the tank. Any ideas or advice would be so appreciated - I'm feeling quite overwhelmed by it currently! Thanks in advance.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/cb024f2003da3e68_7273-w500-h807-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/024255d103da3e69_7277-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/13624dbe03da3e69_7284-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1922680706", "author_name": "Peter Reader Landscapes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1922680706", "date": "2023-02-06", "text": "Hiya Yes long narrow gardens can be quite a challenge and overwhelming at first sight. A couple of comments and suggestions that might help. Firstly, to divide a garden up into rooms you don't necessarily want to have complete screenings across the garden as this really hides the rest of the garden from view. It is much better to have areas of planting coming out into the space and use items of hard landscaping like paths to add the suggestion of rooms. I attach a photo where this has been done very well. Each circular area feels like a room, but is partly visible from elsewhere in the garden. This creates journeys and half-seem focal points that add interest and mystery to the garden as a whole and draw you out to explore it. Within each room there are also hidden quiet spots. Secondly, the best place to hide the circular covers is in one of the beds that come out into the lawn, or even just in the lawn itself, particularly if it is just beside a bed. With all the other distractions going on, you will not notice them nearly as much, if at all. Planting wise, I would not plant a big tree near the sewerage system, but most shrubs would be fine, as would a small tree like an Acer or an Amelanchier. Both are lovely trees. The final option would be to hire a local garden designer to do this planning for you, or even just pay them for a 'design consultation'. A number of designers will charge you an hourly rate to walk around your plot and make high-level suggestions and ideas for you to implement yourself. Good luck with your design.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5122b6e403e0ca5f_6256-w240-h267-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Favorite musical artist? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lettersatoz", "author_name": "lettersatoz", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lettersatoz", "date": "2023-02-01", "text": "Someone asked me in another thread who my favorite musical artist is, when I mentioned I had one.  So as not to derail that thread, and because I think it would be fun to know others' faves, I thought I would start a new one. I am a HUGE fan of music, and my tastes are probably more diverse than most.  I have created workout play lists with tempos to match what I'm doing and if you saw some of the types of music included, you would probably shake your head in confusion.  I made one for a 16 hour car trip I took once too, trying to match songs to the areas we'd be driving through.  As a 57 year old, I will go to my grave defending the 80's as the best musical decade, though there's also lots to love from the 70's and 90's, as well as older stuff and current stuff.  I favor rock and pop, but I even have a classical music station in my car's presets for those moments I'm stuck in horrid traffic and need to calm my nerves.  In the late 70's, during the classic rock vs. disco wars, I fell squarely in the middle, enjoying both. I've never followed country music much, though current country may be changing my mind a little. Anyway.....my very favorite artist is Phil Collins, from his early Genesis stuff through his 80's pop, a little lesser so his 90's stuff, all the way up to his Big Band project, which most people don't even know about.  I all but bore a hole into my Three Sides Live album back in the day and as I mentioned in the other thread, no other artist's music can take me back to exact moments in time like his can.  As a kid, I played the drums for a short time, so maybe I just favor drummers.  There are many youtube clips of him and Chester Thompson (who took over as Genesis' drummer when Phil took over lead vocals) in a drum duet, but this one is one of my faves - so fun to watch! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TAivMqtDJfU So.....who is your favorite, if you have one? We still have to select the veneer stone that will be on the face of the fireplace area and I know that is a consideration for what color we select for the walls. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jennifer-hogan285", "author_name": "Jennifer Hogan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jennifer-hogan285", "date": "2023-02-02", "text": "The conventional wisdom is to choose a neutral that \"works\" with everything and that leaves your options for other colors wide open. For me there are some neutrals that work okay with most everything, but they may not be the best with the colors you love or in some cases they may not even be okay. My favorite colors wine reds and purples.  Those neutrals that they say work with everything usually greige (gray/beige with green undertones)   The neutrals with pink or violet undertones (taupe or violet gray) are the ones that most people steer you away from, but that look great with my colors. My sister loves olive greens and golds and orange reds - classic fall colors. - Greige is great in her home. My sister in law loves cornflower blues and peach.  Greige looks muddy with her pastels, a light, clear cream or a light gray both work well. I am in my 60s and I can remember when we struggled with picking colors for our first homes and buying things through the years that were the popular colors of the day.  At some point we all landed on the colors for in our home that are actually the same color families that look good on us.   I am a winter  (dark hair, ivory skin tone) and look good in bright, clear colors, Susie is a fall, (brown hair, olive skin tone) and looks great in muted greens that make me look like I died a week ago.   Lisa has blond hair and blue eyes and skin that tans as soon as she walks out the door.  Spring pastels look beautiful on her.    We all ended up filling our homes with the colors that make our hearts sing, and apparently we are vain and the colors that made us feel like a 10 when we were young make our hearts sing. main_question: {"author_id": "samuel-mayhew", "author_name": "Samuel Mayhew", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/samuel-mayhew", "date": "2023-02-01", "text": "We have a house built in 1917. I was doing some remodel work in our upstairs guest room. I pulled out lathe and plaster and some old insulation. I realize now that it was likely asbestos insulation. I have already sheetrocked and covered up the area I was working in, swept, vacuumed, had an air purifier running etc. I will test the insulation to see if it is asbestos, but If it is Asbestos then would the fibers stay in the house even after cleaning up everything or if they do then do they go back into the air everytime the furnace kicks on? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gn-builders-l-l-c-pfvwus-pf~1476403835", "author_name": "GN Builders L.L.C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/general-contractors/gn-builders-l-l-c-pfvwus-pf~1476403835", "date": "2023-02-11", "text": "To start with if you have asbestos, you shouldn't sweep or vacuum... the main idea is not to release particles into the air. You should have done testing before you did all that work and found out what the insulation was but now it is what it is. 1st see if it is asbestos, maybe you get lucky and if it is you can rent  A HEPA filter-equipped negative air machine, you can get them at box store rentals, this machine creates negative air pressure and keeps airborne asbestos fibers from leaving the containment. main_question: {"author_id": "spamdavy", "author_name": "spamdavy", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/spamdavy", "date": "2023-02-02", "text": "Hi there, What is a good underlayment for radiant hydronic heating (low R-value, high U-value) that also has good soundproofing (high IIC)? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-02-02", "text": "Can we have specifics on the floor and on the radiant system. What level of noise reduction are you trying to achieve and why (you have a recording studio or just don't want to hear footfalls)? I am most interested in minimizing footfall noise from the upper floor. No recording studio \u2013 I just want to make sure my parents won't be bothered by high energy children running around upstairs. The hydronic radiant system is a staple up system nestled between the ceiling joists. The subfloor on the second floor was constructed in the mid 1900s and I think it's just wooden planks (see attached pic). Insulation is stuffed into the ceiling joists. The ceiling will be double-drywalled with Green Glue soundproofing compound. Still, I understand the underlayment will have the most impact on footfall noise. The engineered wood floors will be compatible with radiant heating. I understand the heating will perform better with tile and stone but will compromise with wood floors. I would not use any type of resilient underlayment system as they generally work by converting sound energy to heat energy and tend to not be conductive to either. title: Woodstove people, what's your technique for a cold start? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "editoria", "author_name": "Alisande", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/editoria", "date": "2023-02-02", "text": "My woodstove, a large Jotul that we bought decades ago, has always been a \"hard start.\" It wasn't a problem when we used to keep the stove going all night, but I stopped doing that when I started living alone, and then every start became a cold start. Over the years I worked out a method that was successful most of the time, starting with crumpled newspaper and split fatwood and ending with a few medium logs, with a couple of other layers in between. Recently my son was giving me a hard time about using newspaper. I was not about to give it up, but I know there are other ways to handle it besides crumpling. So I poked around online and found this: https://www.woodheat.org/top-down-steps.html As you can see, he uses a lot of wood to start with, and ends up with a big fire--bigger than I'd be comfortable with. Still, I was intrigued with his \"top down\" method of building a fire, and gave it a try using less wood. In an earlier post he described \"Nantucket Knots\" made from newspaper by rolling large sheets diagonally and then tying the roll into a knot. My knotted newspaper proved to be rather useless, but when I added a couple of crumpled pieces things got going. It was interesting watching it burn, and I liked how the logs on the bottom provided air flow as opposed to having everything flat on the bottom surface of the stove. Right now I have a larger number than usual of round logs. They vary in thickness, but their tendency to roll makes stacking tricky. I settled on a very much modified \"top down\" method: three medium logs on the bottom with newspaper stuffed between them, then three  pieces of split fatwood, a handful of twigs from the yard, three skinny pieces of ash wood that my son splits for me (I'm a lucky mom), and then a couple of small-to-medium logs. More are added when the fire gets going--which happens quickly. I feel as though the \"hard start\" has finally met its match.  :-) So what's your method?", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-639543985", "author_name": "Mongoose Salty", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-639543985", "date": "2023-02-03", "text": "Hey group, Carrier Performance Series furnace, 2 years old (installed Oct, 2020) has an interesting feature. When the temps get really cold (-20C and below) the furnace will not kick on until I open the lower front panel and close it again. I do nothing else, touch nothing just open and close and away it goes. Any other time other than extremely cold conditions this thing just does it thing.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-95533267", "author_name": "Ron A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-95533267", "date": "2023-02-16", "text": "I have a Bryant high efficiency furnace that has had ongoing issues since I installed it in 2000. It is actually made by Carrier. The door at the bottom has a lockout switch, so I guess it could be as simple as the switch itself not staying in the made position. Or, it could be that your controls are locking out and opening the door causes the controls to be reset. I would suggest checking the window that allows you to see through this door when it has failed to start. If there are any codes set, you will be able to see them without removing the door. The repeated code for I have had for various reasons has been the 42 (4 amber blinks, and then 2 green ones). It means that the inducer fan has not come up to speed in the allowed amount of time. My causes have been rubbing fan impellor, poor bearings, and in one case a plugged condensate drain trap that flooded the inducer housing. In any case check for codes and you will find out if there is anything more serious wrong. You should be able to find a list of codes on line, although there may be a list on the furnace door. To complicate things a little more, I recall that in some cases two codes can be set, and they will only display sequentially once, and after that only the last code is shown. So you have to sit there and watch it and hope it fails while you are still watching it... Not a great system.", "images": []}}

The best houses orient the public rooms towards the south for the best passive solar heating and cooling The best houses are L, U, T, H, or I shaped. The best houses are only one to two rooms deep. And covered lanai, porches, garages, etc count as rooms in this case. The best houses make sure kitchens have natural light, meaning windows so one doesn't have to have lighting 24/7 to use the kitchen. (And no, dining areas with windows 10' or more from the kitchen will not allow for natural light.) The best houses make sure all public rooms and bedrooms have windows on at least two walls. The best houses do not if possible put mechanical rooms, pantries or closets on outside walls The best houses do not have diagonal interior walls making for odd spaces. The best houses keep public and private spaces separate. (Meaning you're not walking into the bedroom directly from a public room) The best houses do not have you walk through the work zone of the kitchen to bring laundry to the laundry room. The best houses do not have the mudroom go through any of the work zones of the kitchen. The best houses do not use the kitchen as a hallway to any other rooms. The best houses do not put toilets or toilet rooms up against bedroom walls or public areas. The best houses do not have walk in closets too small to stand inside. (One needs 2' for hanging space and 32\"-36\" for walking space. Ideally the 36\") The best houses have separation, such as closets, between bedrooms and between bedrooms and public rooms. The best houses do not have roofs that are overly large, and dominate the exterior of the house. The best houses do not have stick on exterior materials only on the front fa\u00e7ade. title: Would you expect an apology of sorts for this situation? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "gw-oakley", "author_name": "Oakley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gw-oakley", "date": "2023-02-04", "text": "I don't expect an apology now, it's only been like 30 years ago.  lol  Back story is when DS1 was around 12, he had some buddies over to spend the night.  At dusk they were outside running around when one of the boys came inside and he could hardly breathe.  As an asthmatic myself I knew immediately he was having an asthma attack so I had him take a puff from my inhaler and he could finally breathe. He went back outside and I called his mom to let her know I think he has asthma and she might take him to the doctor.  She said he doesn't have asthma and didn't appreciate that I had him use an inhaler.  Seriously? Today I had a nice chat with his wife, our pharmacist, and we were talking about old times and I asked if he still had asthma because I never asked about it after it happened.  She said yes, and his lungs are very sensitive and he has to be watched closely due to covid, other illnesses, and excercise induced asthma which DS2 has.  And I was the one who figured out DS2 had it when he was sitting on the grass at baseball practice and could barely breathe while the coach was standing there talking to the guys.  I had to get out of my car to get him. I know, water under the bridge,etc.  But I can't help but wonder why she didn't call and thank me for alerting her.  If the situation was reversed, I'd call and thank her profusely. PSA:  I think everyone should have an Abuterol inhaler at home even if you don't have asthma.  When DH came down with congestive heart failure all of a sudden, his symptom was he couldn't catch his breath.  He doesn't have asthma but I gave him my inhaler to use while I called 911. I've never worked in a restaurant, but I have had some formal training - French cuisine and competition barbecue. But I'd never consider myself to be anything more than a cook. In fact, when someone calls me a chef, I correct them and insist I'm just the guy cooking the meal. It could be that the line of demarcation is presentation - tiny chunks of meat, squiggles of sauce, sprouts placed with forceps, all on a gigantic plate. title: (OT) Winter cleanup | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2023-02-05", "text": "Thank goodness it's winter.  This morning dawned foggy and chilly after a run of mild, mostly sunny weather, the last two days being really springlike:  bad for the environment, good for doing garden maintenance. I've been principally occupied by the delta project.  This is the area where the first drainage ditch in the big garden runs off the property and into the neighbors' woods.  Some years ago it occurred to me that I was losing water, sediment, and nutrients by maintaining the ditch, and the garden would probably be better served if I blocked the ditch instead and allowed the water to spread out, slow down, and drop its sediment on our property where it would feed our roses, and not on the neighbors' land for the benefit of their nettles and brambles.  So I began putting pruned matter in the ditch, and, lo and behold, it worked.  The ditch at the bottom has filled in, the water is spreading more widely.  We had had a crossing, a drainage pipe with grassy soil covering it:  the pipe is completely filled, water flowing over the crossing.  This is a problem, of course.  I went to pruning two of the roses in the area, 'Violacea' and 'Petite Orl\u00e9anaise', both vigorous and badly in need of a cleaning up, and scattered the pruned matter over the crossing and everywhere in the area where it squelched when I walked.  Of course the pruned matter will capture more sediment.  My hope is that in time I'll have a spread of rich, permeable soil through which the water can trickle, without the need for channels.  I don't know whether this is reasonable, but it's fun finding out. The invasive plants down there are fearsome.  I must not have worked much there for a couple of years for them to have gotten to this point, and the delta project with its rich moist soil hasn't helped.  The area is overgrown with nettles, and nettles are terrible.  They root deeply, and then send millions of miles of secondary roots in all directions, at least that's what it feels like; and digging them out of the sticky delta soil is challenging.  After the nettles it will be the brambles, which will be worse.  There's a jungle of them down on the neighbors' property, and they've now reached up into the roses.  Mine to deal with, including the neighboring jungle, just to keep the brambles out of my garden.  I spend many hours maintaining my neighbors' property on this principle, fighting off their brush. I also cleaned up the forsythia and Japanese quince, getting them off each other's throats, and for light relief weeded the herbaceous peonies in the neighboring area and pruned the young figs there.  This area may one day become an attractive garden, if my activities can ever overcome the poor soil and finish the planting.  I'm thinking it may become part of my next fall campaign.  On the principle of never wasting anything, the weeded nettles went on the path there, as the ground is poor and needs extra organic matter.  It's a way of transferring nutrients from the ditch to other areas.  Another advantage of warm sunny weather is that roots die quickly; certainly I don't want more nettles. It's still definitely winter, and I hope will stay so for some weeks more.  Also, after our recent good rains, I'm starting to worry about water again.  Well, patience.  The snowdrops, green and common, down in the woods, are in flower.  The flower buds of Cornelian cherry are showing color; winter aconite, which I would like more of, is in bloom.  The winter jasmine, bright yellow but scentless, is fading, while the shrub honeysuckle is coming into flower, its blooms insignificant but fragrant, detectable at a distance; and the winter flowering cherry is coming into full bloom at last. I'm still low in energy some weeks after catching Covid, so am working in a pottering manner and with frequent rests while stretched out on the grass.  Who knows when I'll get back to normal, but at least I don't have to drag myself off to a paying job, or have demanding care duties at home.  I always feel better for being outdoors. So, people, what have you been doing in the garden?", "images": []}

My idea is to use 1/2 in x 500 ft irrigation tube...like the following: https://www.homedepot.com/p/Rain-Bird-1-2-in-x-500-ft-Drip-Irrigation-Tubing-Coil-T70-500S/204751462 On one end, I'll use a hose connector to connect the tubing to the outdoor faucet.  The other end would tie into copper pipe with a facuet on the end.  I plan to lay the tubing at the bottom of the wooden fence and use little \"U\" shapped pins to hold it on the ground. At the faucet by the above ground garden, I will hook up a drip irrigation system to water the plants. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "krnuttle", "author_name": "krnuttle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/krnuttle", "date": "2023-02-05", "text": "We have a similar system for a  fountain at church. The difference is the pipe is underground.  It works just about all year long, except the months with freezing temperatures. You said you worried about freezing, so I assume you your house is plumbed with Freeze Proof exterior faucets.   It you go with you system make sure that not only the pipe is drained, but also the faucet. https://phyxter.ai/blog/freeze-proof-outdoor-faucet If you leave the hose attached to the faucet during the freezing weather,  it will no longer be freeze proof as the water in the long tube in the faucet will not drain properly. Several years ago, not knowing about the faucets, we nearly flooded the basement of the church when the hose was left attached to the Freeze proof faucet and it froze.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "tvglaser", "author_name": "tvglaser", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tvglaser", "date": "2023-02-07", "text": "Thanks krnuttle", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2023-02-07", "text": "Before I read down to the drip irrigation part, my first thought was to use 350 feet of 1.5-inch PVC.  The benefit of PVC is that it is rigid enough to maintain water pressure all the way out.  The benefit of the larger size is that it will carry a relatively normal flow of water over that distance.  Any farther and I'd go to 2-inch pipe.  If you think you might need to use something besides drip out there someday, the 1/2-inch line won't carry the flow of water you need.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "tvglaser", "author_name": "tvglaser", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tvglaser", "date": "2023-02-07", "text": "Hi, great point.  I had assumed a water hose is 1/2 to 3/4 inch.  Maybe it's the distance that might impact the water pressure.  It is possible we might want to use the water for more than drip irrigation, which is why I had posted this; as I have not done this before.  Thx!", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2023-02-08", "text": "For example, a couple of decades ago I visited a rural setting where cattle were being raised.  They had a raised concrete cistern about 20 feet off the ground with a 1-inch PVC pipe stretching down another 30 feet lower (total of 50 feet of head pressure) over a distance of about 1,000 feet.  They turned on the faucet at the cistern and we drove to the livestock tank where the water was headed.  By the time we got there it was trickling out.  We went about our business evaluating the forage in the pasture and returned past the livestock tank on the way back.  By that time the water was roaring out of the pipe at what you would call, full blast. I don't want to get into the mathematics involved, but in essence, the farther the run, the bigger diameter pipe you want.  Just going from 1/2-inch to 3/4-inch more than doubles the cross sectional area of the pipe and significantly reduces the flow resistance. You also lose pressure when the pipe is flexible.  Drip irrigation pipe doesn't need to be rigid for low pressures, but if you are planning for higher flow someday, then rigid PVC will hold the pressure all the way out.  Flexible pipe expands and there is pressure loss in that expansion.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-37028472070", "author_name": "T. H.", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-37028472070", "date": "2023-02-06", "text": "Hello, I have a problem with my biggest bromeliad. I water it almost only into the cup, just sometimes a little bit to the roots so they wont dry completely. I fertilize less than once in 2 months. Still, leaves of my bromeliad are curling and are their edges at the bottom are turning Brown. I have watered them by water for some time, but now I use predominantly Rain water, however the problems Last.Thank you for any insights.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2023-02-11", "text": "If you are watering primarily in the cup, and supplying a dribble here and there to roots. All fertilizer salts are accumulating in the grow medium, which makes it continually more difficult for the plant to take up and move water efficiently. Eventually, as the level of dissolved solids/ salts in the grow medium continues to increase, water absorption will become impossible, or even act to pull water out of cells, reversing the normal process of osmosis and pulling water OUT of plant cells via the same mechanism curing salts 'pulls' water from the cells of meat destined to become bacon, jerky, ham, ..... . The technical name for what is occurring is 'plasmolysis', but more commonly it's known as fertilizer burn. The fix: Flush the soil on a regular basis. The grow medium looks very dense, so you might need to use something that allows you to flush the soil regularly w/o the need for concern the medium will remain wet too long and cause root issues related to either function or health. Al", "images": []}}

title: Watering roses in winter? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hzdeleted-60638948", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-60638948", "date": "2023-02-07", "text": "Now this is clearly the sort of question that has no one right answer, but I want to start a discussion on the topic to help me decide on how I want to proceed. Up until about the 23rd of January we've had  good rain and even snow here in Tuscany,for which I am profoundly grateful. Now it's been about 2 weeks with no rain, and it's turned cold again -what counts as cold for us-the lowest temperature given on one of my weather sites is to be -5 celsius,with the high at about 3; that is a low of 23 F,high between 37/38F ,but sunny. This is only supposed to last until the weekend, when once more the highs will be around 11-14 C (in the 50s F),the lows only about 30-35 F. Roses don't consider this to be very cold. During the autumn I planted out about 40 potted plants into my garden,and now I'm wondering: should I water them once the temperature goes back up , as it is predicted to do next week? I dare say that the soil is not dry per se-the evaporation rate is still too slow (thank Heaven). However most of my plants are not dormant at all-certainly the roses are not; they are putting out their leaf buds,and some are obviously GROWING (i.e., basal breaks, hoorah). So, how do I regulate myself as far as watering goes?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "catspa-zone9sunset14", "author_name": "catspa_zone9sunset14", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/catspa-zone9sunset14", "date": "2023-02-07", "text": "I do water new autumn plantings if there is a lag in precipitation during the winter (such as happened during the two winters prior to this one here).  Plants recently put into the ground from a pot generally haven't sent roots very far into the surrounding soil, so remain dependent on whatever moisture is in its potting medium.  Potting media are designed to be well-drained and, in my experience, tend to dry out sooner than the ambient soil.  For me, the threshhold during winter is somewhere around three weeks without rain or since the last irrigation.  I keep careful watch on new plantings and poke a finger down into the potting medium to see how dry it is.  Last winter, for example, I remember watering new plantings at least several times and they needed it.", "images": []}}

You should water when the plant needs it. Watering on a schedule, unless you're using a grow medium specifically formulated to allow you to do that, almost always leads to episodes of over or under-watering. Burned leaf tips and/or leaf margins are most often a symptom of a problem in the rootzone. You can determine appropriate watering intervals by using a \"tell\". More on that below. Your plant looks very chlorotic. When did you last fertilize? what did you use? Does the pot have a drain hole? Does it have a collection saucer? Do you allow the plant to reabsorb the water that makes it into the collection saucer? Do you know your home's range of relative humidity? Your plant is sensitive to fluoride and fluoride is accumulative in plant tissues. Low humidity increases transpiration (water loss through the leaves), which speeds up the nutrient stream (water and what's dissolved in that water), which means more fluoride accumulates in leaves under low humidity conditions. Using a 'tell' Over-watering saps vitality and is one of the most common plant assassins, so learning to avoid it is worth the small effort. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering - leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips, rather than resolving a dilemma, simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma. It creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. Leave it a few seconds, then withdraw it and inspect the tip for moisture. For most plantings, withhold water until the tell comes out dry or nearly so. If you see signs of wilting, adjust the interval between waterings so drought stress isn't a recurring issue. Does the pot have a drain hole? If there is a collection saucer, are you allowing the plant to reabsorb the water that collects in it? When is the last time you fertilized? What did you use? How long have you had the plant? Hibiscus are one of the few plants that actually need a special fertilizer; this, because they use more potassium than nitrogen, whereas most plants use around 6x as much N as potassium. Hibiscus use only a very limited amount of phosphorous, so \"bloom-booster-type fertilizers' should always be avoided. Hibiscus also have very aggressive root systems, and need a full repot annually (in mid-spring) to be at their best. When they become seriously rootbound, they often shed inner foliage (close to the trunk) such that in the end all or almost all foliage is concentrated near branch tips. Plants make and store their own energy source \u2013 photosynthate - (sugar/glucose). Functioning roots need energy to drive their metabolic processes, and in order to get it, they use oxygen to burn (oxidize) their food. From this, we can see that terrestrial plants need plenty of air (oxygen) in the soil to drive root function. Many off-the-shelf soils hold too much water and not enough air to support the kind of root health most growers would like to see; and, a healthy root system is a prerequisite to a healthy plant. Watering in small sips in order to avoid over-watering leads to a residual build-up of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil from tapwater and fertilizer solutions - which limits a plant's ability to absorb water \u2013 so watering in sips simply moves us to the other horn of a dilemma and creates another problem that requires resolution. Better, would be to simply adopt a soil that drains well enough to allow watering to beyond the saturation point, so we're flushing the soil of accumulating dissolved solids whenever we water; this, w/o the plant being forced to pay a tax in the form of reduced vitality, due to prolong periods of soil saturation. Sometimes, though, that's not a course we can immediately steer, which makes controlling how often we water a very important factor. In many cases, we can judge whether or not a planting needs watering by hefting the pot. This is especially true if the pot is made from light material, like plastic, but doesn't work (as) well when the pot is made from heavier material, like clay, or when the size/weight of the pot precludes grabbing it with one hand to judge its weight and gauge the need for water. Fingers stuck an inch or two into the soil work ok for shallow pots, but not for deep pots. Deep pots might have 3 or more inches of soil that feels totally dry, while the lower several inches of the soil is 100% saturated. Obviously, the lack of oxygen in the root zone situation can wreak havoc with root health  and cause the loss of a very notable measure of your plant's potential. Inexpensive watering meters don't even measure moisture levels, they measure electrical conductivity. Clean the tip and insert it into a cup of distilled water and witness the fact it reads 'DRY'. One of the most reliable methods of checking a planting's need for water is using a 'tell'. You can use a bamboo skewer in a pinch, but a wooden dowel rod of about 5/16\u201d (75-85mm) would work better. They usually come 48\u201d (120cm) long and can usually be cut in half and serve as a pair. Sharpen all 4 ends in a pencil sharpener and slightly blunt the tip so it's about the diameter of the head on a straight pin. Push the wooden tell deep into the soil. Don't worry, it won't harm the root system. If the plant is quite root-bound, you might need to try several places until you find one where you can push it all the way to the pot's bottom. title: Ideas on creating buffer between drywall and HVAC | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "amanda-giedroc", "author_name": "Amanda Giedroc", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/amanda-giedroc", "date": "2023-02-09", "text": "Recently moved into a new construction home.  A few months ago, we started noticing a loud banging/popping noise in our walls during and after the heat would run.   We brought this up to our builder.  They said the noises in the wall were normal and left it at that.  So, on a weekend when it was really loud, we tore out the drywall where the popping/banging/knocking was loudest and noticed the runs are sitting right up against the drywall. title: Getting Good Flavor when Cooking without Salt | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "funkyartoo", "author_name": "Funkyart", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/funkyartoo", "date": "2023-02-10", "text": "I am preparing a number of items for BIL who had a heart attack and nephew who has stage 5 kidney disease-- both need a low fat/low salt diet (nephew has other restrictions like low phosphorus and low potassium). I know a lot of folks are on low-salt diets for various reasons. but I find low-salt cooking to be so very flat and bland... so I thought I'd tap this great group for guidance, tips and recipes for low-salt cooking that doesn't compromise FLAVOR. The top request from both families was for salad dressings and marinades. I think I have done a pretty good job there. I make a wide array of interesting vinaigrettes -- and I already had glass bottles  (and ordered more).  They eat a fair amount of lean grilled meats -- so to start,  I prepared a greek vinaigrette marinade for chicken and will be making a roasted garlic herb marinade for beef and pork this afternoon (I think I'll add rosemary too). I have plenty of other options..  garlic balsamic vinegar, citrus/garlic. I am pretty comfortable here but please let me know if you have a favorite. I madethis marinara saucewith DOP san marzano tomatoes with no salt in the tomatoes and no salt added to the sauce .. but I really found it was really missing something without salt. I added a touch of sugar. I also increased the oregano and added garlic at the end (despite 14 cloves of garlic to flavor the oil!). I think it is pretty good now .. but I was surprised how much I needed to alter a classic recipe just to make up for salt! I have since read that some people will cook the sauce with a carrot. I'll try that next time. Note: i used the sauce to make a baked chicken parmesan and lean meat sauce for whole wheat pasta. I was tempted to add a parmesan rind to the sauce as \"small amounts\" of parmesan are ok for each but I was concerned that without control of the amount, it would add too much salt. It would certainly add some richness to the sauce though. Do you have any other suggestions or recipes to share? TIA!", "images": []}

title: Latent Defect in New Home | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lasteele", "author_name": "Just Me (Zone 6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lasteele", "date": "2023-02-10", "text": "We built a house almost three years ago and have been happy with it for the most part. The toilet in our guest bathroom on the basement level plugged up this fall, and we ended up calling a plumber after our plunging and snaking efforts failed. He cleared it but also used a camera to see the plumbing run all the way to the street. He showed us that there was a \"belly\" in the run and said it was a contractor error on the build. We contacted the builder who sent us to their plumbing sub and also pointed out that we were past our warranty. We looked online and found a state law that gives us six years to resolve any latent defects in our construction. Long story short, we had the subcontracting plumber and a sewer company here (at the sub's request and cost). They have now determined the piping has no pitch and thus has standing water from the toilet to the backwater valve. We are being told the fix will involve removing the concrete from the toilet outward, thus requiring digging up the floor, toilet and possibly the vanity and bathtub in that bathroom. title: Here's hoping I can prune soil flush on a budded rose | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "a1an", "author_name": "a1an", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/a1an", "date": "2023-02-11", "text": "This year would be year 5 on growing roses. And everytime around  this time of the year, I find myself,  googling, youtubing, seeing what evidence is there that once can prune canes flush to the soil line on grafted roses. While I have pruned them every year, I did so sparingly, as in my mind, these were -new roses- and the more leaves the better. ALOT of these roses seems to have really large *main stems* with 2-3 branch WYES and branching from them. The large main stems are probably the main stems from when I received them. I do have new canes, but these seems to be coming off the *WYE* of the larger main canes. When at see the video's of pruning, I see shrubs with -many- singular canes comeing from soil line. I suppose either these are established roses and or these are -own root roses- , as there appears to be many singular canes. I did a quick survery and only a -handful- of mind, I can clearly see new comes from soil line that are not off what I'm calling -main stems WYES- from original planting 5 years back. This year, I finally did it. I took out one large WYE flush to the soil, as the canes were growing crossing into it. On another shrub, I noticed 2 stems stems  that was of decent girth , so I cut a older barkier one flush to the soil line. The barkier one did take out another *WYE* and maybe it may be missing a -hole- on one side of the framework now, but I'm going to see if the energy will now be displaced and new canes will come out from the soil line .", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2023-02-12", "text": "I'm always struck by how germination speeds for different vegetables differ. I have pots where I'm starting peppers, cukes, and squash. Peppers are always very slow. Three weeks after planting they're barely an inch tall. Cukes are faster. They're there after two weeks. Squash? BLAM! They're two inches tall a week after planting. Planning to meet last-frost day outside always requires some care in planting schedule. Mine is third week in February.  New gardeners often aren't aware of this.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "zeedman", "author_name": "zeedman Zone 5 Wisconsin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/zeedman", "date": "2023-02-21", "text": "\" I usually plant pointy-end down, but you're right, planting them flat  should be OK. But you're saying that pushing up through more soil better  removes the seed coats?\" I think that anything which speeds germination results in more issues with clinging seed coats. I've observed this with cucurbits planted pointy-end down; those planted flat had little to no problem. This was most noticeable with bitter melon & other gourds. This problem was also noticeable with tomatoes germinated at high temperatures (about 85 F.) When I germinate them at 70-75 F., I see far fewer helmets. I've also seen this in okra, which germinates in 3-4 days when started in pots (with A LOT of helmets) and germinates in 6-7 days in-ground, with few helmets. I think that in both cases, the extra time in moist soil before emergence helps to both soften the seed coat, and allow the cotyledons more time to break free. Old seed tends to have more clinging seed coats too, regardless of how they are planted.", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "bry911", "author_name": "bry911", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bry911", "date": "2023-02-14", "text": "@HU-458010923 - You should never look at the profit or commission that someone gets for providing a benefit or service to you.  It is a recipe for bad decisions.  The value that someone creates for you is separate from the profit they make from doing it. Because insurance adds administrative and sales costs to spreading risk it will always look bad in the aggregate.  I have never had a home owner's claim, but I still have insurance.  Aside from my annual physical and a colonoscopy, I have only seen my doctor half a dozen times since I was 18... so I have wasted money on health insurance too. main_question: {"author_id": "ashley-foote55", "author_name": "Ashley Foote", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ashley-foote55", "date": "2023-02-13", "text": "The home we moved into last year that has an Electrolux oven (model E36DF76GPS2) This oven is out of warranty, it was purchased several years ago but I also know that the previous owners had it setting in storage for a long time before it was put in the house we now live in. Sometimes you can turn the over back on after a few min. and it works fine & other times it will continue doing the same thing. We had a tech come out Feb 2022 & he told us it was an oven sensor & range relay board. Parts were out of stock though his vendor so we ordered via Ebay with part numbers direct from manufacture. Both were replaced March 2022 and everything worked great for about Oct/Nov then slowly started happening more and more frequently. Now its almost to the point that the oven is almost useless. Had another tech come out (a different company) who confirmed it is the same parts again) but mentioned something about hardwiring something within the range that could fix the issues. He wanted to talk to the manufacture for other options first. but said he has fixed other Electrolux oven issues by doing this in the past. Said it would keep trying to reach them (this was the week of Christmas & he was on hold for 20+ min. while at my home) Can't talk back to tech since his 'main office' won't allow me to, just say the ticket is closed. title: DEKTON Scam?  Dekton super fragile on the edges. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "crsimon1", "author_name": "crsimon1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/crsimon1", "date": "2023-02-14", "text": "Dekton is being sold as the latest and greatest.  No question that it is beautiful and is impervious to scratches and abrasions.  But it is super fragile on the edges.  We've had it for 3 months and have 3 chips already.  And we are two adults, no children and super careful.  It was sold and installed by home depot.  No one is talking about this issue and people are buying it thinking it is indestructible.  Would love to hear your experience.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "denrock-avenue", "author_name": "Amy Owen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/denrock-avenue", "date": "2023-05-11", "text": "We installed Dekton Laurent in our renovation last year. It is stunning...I love the matte leather finish and the warm brown veining. Everyone who walks into my home, loves it. Dekton makes the largest slab on the market so we could do our island without any top seams...which was a huge plus. But buyers beware. Our kitchen, with a huge waterfall island, butler pantry & servery required 6 slabs so it was one of the higher ticket items in our project. We are 2 careful adults and have, in one year's time, had 6 chips in this material. The first & so far, worst one was caused by a $10 ceramic dog treat jar tapping the edge of the island...when I heard the \"thunk\" I thought for sure I broke the ceramic, only to look down and see the chip in the edge. I nearly threw up...we had only been back in the house for a month when it happened. We have 2 chips along the bottom edge of the bar, where I guess the stools hit it when being lifted back into place. There is even one in the flat surface of a backsplash, almost like slate will chip off flat bits of its surface. This one is located where the (wall) splash meets the countertop, so it is not a vulnerable edge. If that isn't the fabrication, I'm not sure how we could have caused it...? When we got to chip #4, we started calling the Consentino showroom. Because we also had issues with the cut around the flush mount Miele induction HOB being so poorly done, we were convinced that our fabricator was perhaps the cause, or as @Sabrina Alfin Interiors suggested, used the wrong/dull blades.. (we did not choose the fabricator, he was part of the kitchen team that our kitchen contractor \"always uses\"...and he was paid separately and directly...another story/lesson learned). While questioning his qualifications for working with the material, he of course, was never able to provide us with his Dekton Certification for having completed the special training required by Consentino. (although I was told that he would not have been able to purchase the slabs without it...yeah, right). My husband and I both work for large, well-known architecture firms and had to use the full weight of our professional stature to get a Consentino rep to our home to see what was happening. She came, said next to nothing to us, took some pictures. Months went by and we heard nothing. After many calls and emails, she finally responded by emailing a link to the product specs, fabrication instructions & their joke of a warranty...ALL things that I already had downloaded from their website. They were basically saying \"we don't care\". We have threatened that no Cosentino material will ever be specified by either of our firms again. Did not matter. They will not admit to any flaw in this product and would not confirm our suspicions that poor fabrication tools & techniques could/would cause [additional] vulnerabilities or weakness. So we are just left to think about the expense and inconvenience that we will inevitably face to replace all of our countertops...ugh...and just feel sick all over again. Until Consentino addresses the issues and/or makes restitution to those of us who have had problems with this material, we've sworn to let as many people as possible know that it is definitely flawed!", "images": []}}

title: Help with roses | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lclark21324", "author_name": "L Clark (zone 4 WY)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lclark21324", "date": "2023-02-14", "text": "I have some roses in pots that I was storing in my unheated greenhouse for the winter which I then covered in styrofoam cones. So pots heeled in the ground with thick styrofoam cones covering them. I keep a couple roses under styrofoam cones outside not in a greenhouse and it works great. I thought, cones + greenhouse would make for the most superior protection I can offer. Well, in the greenhouse under the cones the roses got insanely moldy. White mold covering everything. Ugh! I didn't check them for like two months which was another bad mistake on my part. Anyway, I think I lost a couple of them as there appears to be no life in the canes (black and mushy!), but a couple appear to have some life in them. We still have a lot of winter yet to go here including some forecast below zero temps. I am worried, in their weakened state, if I leave the roses in the greenhouse subjected to these low temps for the rest of winter the roses will say NO MAS and give up the ghost. My question is can I bring them inside right now, put them in a sunny window and keep them inside for a few months? I am thinking that I may be able to save them if I can bring them out of dormancy now and nurse them back to health asap. Then get them outside once the weather warms. Good idea or bad idea? Sorry for the long post.", "images": []}

The crux of the post removed was that it is ridiculous to think it matters when one chooses to repot their houseplants. What I wrote below is a refutation of that idea, and lists some of the reasons why the suggestion doesn't hold water. *********************************************************************************** No one I know of has ever said the only month appropriate for repotting houseplants is June. You are as free to avoid repotting as long as you like, or choose to repot whenever you like, just as you are free to avoid changing the oil in your car for as long as you like or fill the gas tank only when you feel like it, regardless of how much fuel it contains. The fact is, house plants not grown under lights normally vary significantly in their level of vitality throughout the growth cycle. Stored energy begins to wane quite predictably in mid to late fall, and continues to diminish until after the vernal equinox. What IS ridiculous, is suggesting that repotting when the plant's energy reserves are at their lowest and the plant's current ability to synthesize food/energy remains limited by short days and low light intensity, is not inferior to waiting a bit for the opportunity to work in sync with the plant's natural rhythms and taking advantage of the plant's strengths while making allowances for their weaknesses. I have repotted (fully repotted) many thousands of plants and I can say with a great deal of certainty that most tropicals which are reasonably healthy and repotted or divided somewhere around the summer solstice will recover in a small fraction of the time (a week or two to see new growth) it would take the same plant to recover were it repotted in winter or early spring. I'll reiterate that no one needs permission to repot their plants whenever they please, but that does not mean that the degrees of comparison from poor to middling to good, better, and best time to repot do not apply. One might consider running a marathon after a week-long drinking binge, but it's probably going to turn out better if one makes an allowance for the lack of verve and wait for a better opportunity. I agree the best time to repot changes somewhat with the grower's geographical proximity to the equator, and being nearer than 20* N or S latitude to the equator significantly broadens the period of time that can be considered the best time to repot when viewed from the plant's perspective, but there are still good times and not as good times to repot. Keep in mind too, that repotting is much more involved than potting-up, a practice that isn't as stressful in the immediate, but gradually adds to the accumulative stress that comes with the center of the root/soil mass becoming increasingly congested. Even if we take at face value that someone's winter has been exceptionally warm and sunny and mild, and humidity has been just wonderful, conditions are just starting to gain momentum on the upswing. Unless the plant is in steep decline, we can expect it's level of vitality to continue to improve (where you live) from now until late summer, so the plant would still be the better for a bit of patience. A plant's ability to defend itself against insect herbivory and disease pathogens is a byproduct of it's metabolic processes. A repot now or in the middle of winter ensures a longer recovery and greater susceptibility to insects and diseases during that recovery than if the repot was undertaken when the plant is at peak vitality levels. If someone wants to repot now or in the middle of winter as a show of defiance, that's fine with me. I would just hope that others understand the benefits of working with a plant's natural rhythms instead of at cross purposes with them. Al", "images": []}}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hzdeleted-19706790", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-19706790", "date": "2023-02-15", "text": "Interesting property, looks like great bird habitat! I don't know if you're total newbies with regard to managing a woodland area or not, but here's some considerations. Poison Ivy - make sure you identify it and removing it safely. Small-ish vines can be squirted with Round Up; larger vines you might need to cut off near the ground and use the Round Up as new leaves come out. Once you've gotten rid of it, you're not done. Birds will bring seeds in and new poison ivy plants will spring up, so once a month or so walk your property and look for baby poison ivies -- easy to get rid of when they're only a few leaves high. Other invasive vines - honeysuckle and english ivy are the most common. Persistence is the key -- cut near the base, pull out what comes easily, do it again in a few weeks. English ivy laughs at Round Up so don't even try that. When your tree people come, see if they'll cut some of the trunks into 5 or 6 foot sections and leave them for you. They'll make good edges of pathways, and can help prevent erosion if you place them across the slope. Maybe they can mulch the rest of the oak branches and scatter it in your woods. And if you can get a tree expert to walk your woods with you and identify species, that's great -- you'll enjoy it a lot more if you know what you own. As to clearing areas ... yes that's likely to cause erosion, so have a plan in place before you start. A stop-gap measure could be to plant Winter Rye on any bare soil -- that stuff sprouts very easily, but it won't over-winter so it's only a temporary fix. If that were my woodland, I'd clear out the invasives, plant more natives, add a bird bath near the house, make a few rambling paths through the woods. Leave most of it as \"woodland\" complete with undergrowth; don't try to make it into a park. main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-436863303", "author_name": "Eileen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-436863303", "date": "2023-02-15", "text": "Is anyone into making their own crackers? Last week I made crackers for the first time.  They're fun to make.  I loved working with the warm water dough and was very pleased with the results. After making them twice in one week, I bought a perforated half sheet pan, so I am committed to making them regularly and trying other recipes. I'd like to try a cheddar cheese cracker next. Do you have any favorite cracker recipes to share? This is the recipe I used. I'll add the link but this is my tweaked version and it's half the recipe.  It makes about thirty 2x3\" crackers.  I served them with hummus for Super Bowl but they're also great on their own. Parmesan Sesame Crackers 1 c. flour (120 grams of King Arthur flour)3 tablespoons finely grated parmesan cheese1 tbsp. poppy and sesame seeds (eyeball it)1/2 tsp. baking powder1/4 tsp. salt (I use a rounded 1/4 teaspoon.)1/4 tsp. sugar 1/4 tsp. garlic powder 1/4 - 1/3 c. warm water (I haven't needed the full 1/3 c.) 2 tbsp. + 2 tsp. oil (You can use garlic oil made by sauteing chopped garlic in the oil in the recipe and straining the oil. I topped my first batch of crackers with Everything Bagel mix but didn't care for the toasted garlic flakes in it.)Topping: Sesame seeds, poppy seeds, parmesan cheese, coarse salt Stir together the flour, parmesan, seeds, baking powder, salt, sugar, and garlic. Stir oil into warm water and add to the flour mixture  in  small amounts. Work into dough as you would a pie crust. Don't try to roll these out on parchment paper--it slides around. Dust countertop with 1 tbsp. of flour. Dump dough onto counter and knead about 10  times. Form dough into an oblong and pat it flat into a rectangle. Roll out  into a 9 x 12\" rectangle, about 1/8\" thick. Lift  dough as you roll it to prevent sticking. Pick up dough and place on parchment paper. Reshape but don't worry about making a perfect rectangle. Brush top  lightly with a little oil. Sprinkle additional sesame seeds, poppy seeds, parmesan cheese, and  coarse salt over dough. Go light on the salt. Press topping lightly into  the dough. Place on cookie sheet and score into 2 x 3\" rectangles. A pizza cutter works well. Prick crackers  with a fork. Bake at 400 degrees for 15-18 minutes. Crackers are done when they are  uniformly golden brown on top and bottom. Watch carefully the last few minutes. Remove any outer  crackers that are browning faster. If crackers aren't crisp enough, they can be recrisped in the oven. https://www.tasteofhome.com/recipes/parmesan-sesame-crackers/", "images": []}

title: Rust stains coming from spa jets - pool is 2 1/2 years old | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "chris-bell1060", "author_name": "Chris Bell", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chris-bell1060", "date": "2023-02-16", "text": "We've been wrestling with this issue for a while now and have talked to our pool contractor who naturally claimed he has 'never seen anything like this before'. Basically, we have rust coming from 3 jets our built-in spa  AND rust coming out of one of the return jets in the main pool. What we have done so far: New construction pool. 2.5 years old and this has been occurring for at least a year. I have my theories as to what the issue is, but would love to hear from anyone in here.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/10e2383103ee4bbb_1341-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~881695109", "author_name": "Mystic Pools, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~881695109", "date": "2023-02-19", "text": "OK. This is not a water chemistry issue, Sounds like your diligent in the chemistry management. You're one of the few!! When we set our plumbing either in the spa or the pool, we have to support the pipe by tying it to a piece of rebar. The pipes are stubbed out beyond the shotcrete. After the shot, the crew will carve out around the pipes to allow for access to the pipe to cut them back prior to plastering. I'll post a pic of a recent build during construction to see the stubbed pipes. Most times we have to chip a bit more to allow the wall fitting to sit back far enough to finish flush with the plaster. Sometimes the supporting piece of rebar interferes and we will cut it out. The pipe is cut back and the wall fitting is set. Everything is pre-measured to ensure the fitting when glued is fully seated and ends flush for plaster. Setting the wall fittings should be the PB's responsibility. Not the plaster contractor. Perhaps in your case the rebar was exposed, the pipes were cut back too far, not extended and the plaster contractor set the wall fittings flush as they were plastering. So now the wall fitting is not glued to the stub and the space in between has the rebar exposed resulting in rust. It will never stop. Chipping out the wall would be a great undertaking and any plaster patching would be noticeable. I don't have eyes on these wall fittings, but perhaps cleaning up the affected areas, allow to dry, reach into the fittings and rough the plastic surface with some emery cloth. A long, narrow wire brush attachment may work well. Wipe it clean and apply some GE Silicone where there is a gap. This may be tricky if it's in deep. A long flat applicator of some sort will help. Apply enough to fill the gap but not too much interfere with the jet function. Allow 24 hrs to set. This won't be a permanent fix, but it should stop the rusting issues.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/94a2db4503f21de2_1746-w240-h320-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Miele Dishwasher F12 F13 Error Code | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kari-kus", "author_name": "Kari G", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kari-kus", "date": "2023-02-16", "text": "I recently had the F12 and F13 error codes on my Miele dishwasher.  The fix was changing the water supply hookup. It was originally pulling the water supply from the hot water connection of my sink.  After testing the water temperature, I found out I had my water heater set too high.  Miele can only be hooked up to hot water if the temperatures do not exceed 140 degrees F.  I moved the supply line to the cold water connection and the error code has gone away. Miele has a built in water heater so it does not need to be hooked up to hot water.  (User manual states either hookup is fine as long as hot temperature does not exceed 140 degrees).  It is also more energy efficient hooked up to cold water because it will not constantly be using hot water if cold is called for in the cycle.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-928827909", "author_name": "Jameszone7a Philadelphia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-928827909", "date": "2023-02-18", "text": "Anyone have one ? I am just curious if it\u2019s great marketing or you\u2019ve found these things to be true.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/c922488303f0f705_6271-w500-h1082-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-02-18", "text": "I haven't grown that cultivar but I have grown a number of other oakleaf hydrangeas and recommend them frequently for clients. They are by far my favorite type of hydrangea! With enough sun exposure, ALL oakleafs develop great fall color and recent breeding programs have focused on maximizing that and developing more compact selections. Jetstream appears to be somewhere in between a full sized oakleaf cultivar and the more compact or dwarf forms. It is too big for my current garden but I'd consider growing Jetstream in a container to keep it a bit smaller. Should be a strong performer in zone 7.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "luis-pr", "author_name": "luis_pr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/luis-pr", "date": "2023-02-18", "text": "I used to have one many years ago but swapped it for a smaller cultivar. The fall color of the foliage was awesome but then, that is common in all of the oakleaf hydrangeas that I have had. The best fall color show happens when it got some morning and afternoon fall sun during the cooler fall temperatures.  Its planting location received very little direct sun (corner spot with two fences on two sides, one big holly on the 3rd side and a big Crape Myrtle providing shade on top) but always bloomed well (common on oakleaf hydrangeas too) and had nice fall colors. Enjoy! Very drought tolerant here in Texas 8a but do not let it sit in wet soil for too long or you will be sorry as they can easily catch root rot. I have no idea how they measure \"stronger\" branches; I did not notice anything specially stronger though. The blooms are smaller compared to other oakleaf varieties and thus, they did not flop in my 'well protected from winds/storms' location.", "images": []}}

In the fall I took a load of cuttings and left them in pots of sand in a sheltered spot in the courtyard. Today is the first day I have checked on them in months and every stem at least has some budding with some stems having buds developing into small leaves. Does this mean every stem has rooted? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "strawchicago", "author_name": "strawchicago z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/strawchicago", "date": "2023-02-20", "text": "Agree with Paul Barden, yesterday Sunday 2/19/23 it got up to 50 F in my zone 5a. I pulled out a bunch of green sticks (with tiny leaves) and ALL OF THEM have ZERO roots, despite rooting them since Nov. 2022.  That's 4 months of rooting.  Hard wood rootings (done through winter) are very slow in forming roots. The very few rootings that have decent roots:  these have 4 to 7 set of full leaflets.  But these winter-roots are not as long as summer-roots.  I took these rootings out of the fabric pouches after I saw roots coming out at bottom.  CONCLUSION:  Unless there's at least 4 set of full-leaflets like below, there are not enough roots on the stem to pull out.  Winter roots are wimpier than summer roots.  Winter rooting can't handle dense medium like sharp sand.   I lost countless cuttings when I tested different combo with sharp sand, such as 100% sharp sand (topped with fertile clay),  1/2 sharp sand and 1/2 vermiculite, or 1/4 sharp sand with 3/4 Pro-mix potting soil and perlite.  Their stems stay green, but THEY FAILED TO FORM ROOTS. The only medium that wimpy winter roots can push through is VERY FLUFFY like at least 1/2 perlite. A friend who rooted INDOOR through her zone 6 winter, with Grow-lights told me the same.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4ef2840103f39c55_9666-w240-h320-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

To try and change that large a space over to a weed free groundcover would be setting yourself up for a lifetime of aggravation. title: softest grass underfoot? for coastal southern california | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dca55", "author_name": "dca55", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dca55", "date": "2023-02-18", "text": "Hi, we're putting a small lawn in our home a couple blocks from the ocean in La Jolla (San Diego). The weather is mild year round (50-80 degrees), and the lawn will get pretty decent sunlight. Kids but no pets.Number one priority is softness for walking on barefoot, but we also of course want it to hold up well, be easy to maintain, look good most of the year, etc.We were thinking maybe a hybrid bermudagrass or maybe something like Zeon Zoysia. The guy at West Coast Turf suggested Platinum TE seashore paspalum. We'd be very grateful to hear what the experts on here think, thank you!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dchall-san_antonio", "author_name": "dchall_san_antonio", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dchall-san_antonio", "date": "2023-02-21", "text": "Thanks for your location.  In 20+ years on this site I can't remember anyone from La Jolla writing in.  Laguna is about as close to a coastal similar location.  Usually people will tell us they are in San Diego, but when you ask, they are often east of Grosmont, which, as you know, is nothing like the San Diego climate, so different turf types are required.  Are you in the area which gets late night and morning low clouds and fog? Have you walked your neighborhood to find lawns that you really like? Are you going to have someone care for it or are you caring for it? If you are caring for it, how much work are you willing to do for mowing and watering?  Mowing ranges from every 3 days for a short, hybrid bermuda to every other week for St Augustine or a hybrid buffalo. Before you go with West Coast Turf's suggestion, ask them to give you some addresses where their turf is installed. Check around to see if UC Verde buffalo grass is available.  One of the keys to underfoot comfort is not having seed stalks sticking up.  Seeded buffalo and even other hybrids can get seed heads.  I believe the UC Verde does not get them, but check to be sure.  UC Verde might only be available online, so ask around.  This grass is possibly the most drought resistant variety.  Bermuda is similarly good, but it has other issues with maintenance. TIF 419 bermuda is a contractor grade turf, but don't let that sway you away.  It is also the gold standard of hybrid bermudas.  The reason contractors use it is that it is raised by the square mile up in Hemet/Winchester, and is super easy to get a lot of fast. When you buy sod you want to buy from someone who sells lots of pallets of it every day.  For example Lowe's and Home Depot sell sod, but they might only sell 5 pallets in 2 weeks.  My local sod outlet in San Antonio sells 14 pallets every day with new grass delivered nightly.", "images": []}}
