The problems of finding clones of great age and inferring their continuity are substantial. When we look at arctic treelines around the world, we find that they sometimes experience primarily clonal reproduction (where the treeline species are capable of it), and sometimes sexual reproduction. The null hypothesis would be that sexual reproduction is episodic over time, occurring during climatic warm intervals that favor complete cone and seed development, with reversions to clonal reproduction during less favorable periods. Therefore, absent evidence to the contrary, the Swedish trees do not represent a 9,000-year-old clone, and the oldest clonal age in this species remains unknown. title: Martha's Spinach Folly | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "docmommich", "author_name": "docmommich", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/docmommich", "date": "2023-02-21", "text": "I have had a dramatic change in my life situation, as many might be aware. So, I have left medicine, gotten divorced, and am living with and caring for my mother on the 11+ acres we've owned for 50+ years. I am developing both vegetable gardens and pollinator habitat throughout the property. One of my fun goals for this spring is to plant and grow as much spinach as I can possibly manage, since everyone in our family loves everything spinach. I want to make spanikopita, spinach dip, quiches, vegetarian lasagna, etc. My plan is to dehydrate as much as I can, since that worked well this year, on a smaller scale. So, yesterday, I was asking my mom what her first choice/favorite thing would be to have planted in a garden. She said she always enjoyed the first few sugar snap peas, but didn't really need more than a few. I asked if she was looking forward to spinach, and in what form. She said, and I quote, \"You mean Martha's Folly?\" Apparently, she doesn't believe that it is possible to grow the quantities of spinach I have in mind. I don't know how she thinks grocery stores manage to maintain their supplies, but I am clearly not up to the job. It doesn't matter that she complained all summer about the excessive quantities of succulent tomatoes and peppers, and the bowls of sugar snap peas that went into the compost pile. It's disheartening, to say the least, when you give up your previous comfortable (though also tortuous) life and set out on a new path, only to have those you count on to support you, belittle your efforts. Sorry to whine, but I thought I might find at least a few sympthetic ears here. I will continue on my quest. Fortunately, I had the opportunity to visit with my son this week (before the Folly comment occurred) and he mentioned spontaneoulsy that feeding my loved ones is my \"Love Language.\" (Of course I had brought him a care package of  homemade green tomato salsa, applesauce, dehydrated mangos, and cherry oatmeal cookies). Not to mention the fact that the skills of small scale food prodection and preservation have been lost to a large swath of society, and deserve to be retained and passed on. Anyone heard of the \"Local Food Movement?\" Blah, blah, blah. Of course my mother is ignorant, but it hurts to have her so oblivious to the value of what I am striving to do. Then again, I'm 57 years old. Why should I care what she thinks? Though she is paying the bills, while I do the laundry, etc. End of rant. title: Moving an established rose | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "hzdeleted-21921585", "author_name": "User", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/hzdeleted-21921585", "date": "2023-02-21", "text": "So I have a potted rose that has rooted through the pot and into the ground.  It's grafted, so it's the rootstock that has rooted through.  I'd like to move it.  What's the best way to do it to ensure minimal damage or shock?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "roseseek", "author_name": "roseseek", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roseseek", "date": "2023-02-21", "text": "The easiest on you and the rose is to sever the roots at the pot holes, prune the top back in balance with the root ball then plant is as a normal canned plant. Trying to retain the roots grown into the ground and more of the top growth is going to be difficult on you and if you're unsuccessful in balancing the top and bottom growth, the top will die back to what the roots can support. If you want, you can literally bare root it so there is no soil ball and the only top growth remaining is what you had when it was a bare root. That way, the feeder roots as well as anchor roots will spread out into a larger area than they may have if you left the potted root ball intact. As long as you keep it hydrated and protected from any hot sun (presuming you're getting any of that right now - we aren't) and drying winds, it will resurrect and grow. Ideally, just after planting, you will receive rains to thoroughly water it in and push new growth quickly.", "images": []}}

Souvenir de la Malmaison is always in flower; Louise Odier, Mme Ernest Calvat, and Mme Isaac Pereire are still babies but very happy ones. Our climate is quite humid but I can overlook a bit of mildew and balling as these roses are such good flowerers for us, even during our very hot, dry summers. My criteria are: - good rebloomer - heat tolerant - climbing (any size) or which can be trained horizontally along a fence or trellis - a bonus would be thornless or low thorn (other than Zephirine Drouhin and Kathleen Harrop) I'd love to hear more about the roses on my shortlist (based on minimal research and lots of swooning over gorgeous photos) or any other suggestions: Comtesse de Rocquigny Souvenir of Mme Auguste Charles Souvenir du President Lincoln Paul Verdier Monsieur Boncenne La Reine Victoria Deuil de Docteur Reynaud Adam Messerich Grazie!", "images": []}

All are own-root.  Don't know about 'Louise Odier' yet, but all the rest get a bit of PM early in the season, though it doesn't last long. I have only had 'Comtesse de Rocquigny' for 3 years, but she has been vigorous and seems to take the heat well. I am growing her as a pillar.   First blooms have balled in the dampness of spring, but she reblooms well and I am very much looking forward to seeing what she does this year, now that she has some size and more developed canes. Another one I am looking forward to for the coming year, now that, finally, we're having a decent amount of winter rain. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kaseki", "author_name": "kaseki", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kaseki", "date": "2023-02-24", "text": "Heh.  You have come to the right place, but my finger callouses may wear off if I have to repeat everything written here that answers your questions.  (Yours probably won't fall off doing all the necessary searching, but to get you started, here are some salient rules that I suggest will be appropriate.) Hood functions include capture and containment.  Capture is enveloping the rising and expanding cooking effluent plumes so that they don't spread out into the room  Containment is transporting the partially filtered effluent to (usually) the outside. One might surmise that capture implies a hood larger than the cooking surface, and for wall hoods not over 36 inches above the cooktop this requirement can be met by a hood at least 3 inches wider than the cooktop each side, and extending at least 3 inches forward of the cooktop (depending on where the elements/burners/hobs are actually located).  Some forward size might be avoided if hot oil cooking occurs on back burners or the hood has side skirts or cabinets helping the flow field move forward a bit. For residential hoods, I recommend an actual 90 CFM per square foot of hood entry (capture) area.  This will require in CFM units a blower achieving the hood entry area (sq. ft.) times 90 ft/min air flow.  The rated (zero static pressure) blower flow rate should be about 1.5 times this CFM. Ducting should be sized to keep full-power actual flow velocity between 1000 and 2000 ft/min. No air leaves the kitchen that isn't replaced.  This replacement is called make-up air (MUA).  Code requires it, and avoiding various undesirable effects demands it.  MUA can be passively (no blower) or actively (with blower) supplied, depending on what pressure loss is safe for any combustion appliances (e.g., dryer, hot water heater) you have connected directly or indirectly to kitchen air instead of having their own MUA, or not having any (e.g., electric hot water heater).  Active MUA will be needed with sensitive combustion appliances, and also the fireplace if you intend to cook vigorously when operating it.  Else, passive may do. MUA should have means of heating it unless you would be willing to cook in winter with the windows open. For background, review the last decade's hood and MUA threads here.", "images": []}}

But it is offset by a reduced time in the motor starting. However the hard start kit determines when the start capacitance value is reduced and the winding current drops down to its reduced amount. title: Excess weight, obesity more deadly than previously believed | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "foodonastump", "author_name": "foodonastump", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/foodonastump", "date": "2023-02-24", "text": "Kind of an interesting study. I'll try to summarize without butchering this: Many previous studies have considered BMI at a moment in time rather than how they've lived over time. So for instance, if you develop an illness due to being overweight and that illness causes you to lose weight rapidly and die, your BMI is considered at time of death and you're reported at low BMI. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "roseseek", "author_name": "roseseek", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/roseseek", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "What attracts pollinators most efficiently are exposed anthers and stamen. Nature favors single flowers because they possess the greatest concentration of stamen with anthers, therefore the most pollen. Pollinators are after the pollen and/or any nectar the bloom forms. Yes, pollinators will visit less single types in efforts to access their anthers, but you'll have the most reliable activity with single to semi single blooms.", "images": []}}

title: Hellebores for the beginner and the limited. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "eleanor-grant85", "author_name": "Eleanor Grant", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/eleanor-grant85", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "I have a small woodland yard in zone 5 Indiana, Lafayette.  I would like to plant hellebore, but I want to know if it is worth it. I tried it before, but it was not successful.  Now I have some serious back issues, and can't dig like I used to. What I have been doing is trying to get natural plants to grow; I have very clayey soil, but we mow all our leaves and leave them in place. So far all my plant friends seem to like this. I do have a semi-sunny patch which gets a lot of sun in winter.  Advice?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "gardengal48", "author_name": "gardengal48 (PNW Z8/9)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/gardengal48", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "The types of hellebores artinnature is referring to with upward and outward facing flowers are intersectional hybrids with rather complex parentage. Although any hellebore is a great garden plant, these ones tend to be a bit limited in coloring as well as seldom featuring any double flowers. Unlike the vastly more common Helleborus x hybridus or \"oriental hybrids\" (with nodding, downward facing flowers in a vast array of colors), these intersectional varieties tend to have white, cream or pink/mauve flowers or a blend thereof.  These are not as common in nurseries and garden centers as the xhybridus but are easily available via mail order. They often have stunning patterned or marbled foliage as well FWIW, all hellebores are easy to grow. All they require is proper drainage and enough sun to promote flowering. While hellebores are shade tolerant, they grow beautifully in quite a lot of sun as long as protected from intense summer heat. Corsican hellebore, H. argutifolius, can be grown in full sun as that is its native condition. Not as hardy as some other varieties however.", "images": []}}

title: How often do peppers cross pollinate? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "docmommich", "author_name": "docmommich", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/docmommich", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "I had always thought peppers were quite likely to cross pollinate. So, in order to save pure seed for growing peppers in future years, I thought the plants or flowers needed to be isolated to prevent bees from mixing the DNA with nearby peppers. There have also been multiple threads on this site where folks discuss the odd peppers they have growing, and knowledgeable posters advise that the pepper seeds must have been from peppers whose flowers where cross pollinated the year before. However, I have been going down rabbit holes online and found several (at least three today) sites that are recommending simply saving seeds from the mature peppers you harvest from your diverse pepper patch. This includes the \"Pepper Geek\" site, which I thought was pretty scientifically rigorous. What actual experience do any of you have when attempting to grow seeds saved from peppers which have not been isolated, but have been grown near other peppers? Martha", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "beesneeds-pfvwus-pf~278115867", "author_name": "beesneeds", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/not-specified/beesneeds-pfvwus-pf~278115867", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "I've had peppers cross. Not such a biggie when it's something like two colors of a similar swet pepper or heat level of hot pepper. I've seen some color mutations or shape irregularities. Not so great if I want a pepper for particular qualities and they get lost. While peppers are self fertile, they also can be pollenated by outside influence like pollinators and weather. If a grower wants to ensure the purity of that pepper, they isolate some or all of it. I isolate by bagging a branch or cluster of buds before they start to bloom. Or I might grow one plant in isolation. I've seen local growers of produce isolate off a small section of plants out of their field. They cage in a few plants at the end of a row to save their seed for the next season.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "outpaientzero", "author_name": "outpaientzero", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/outpaientzero", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "Just saving the seeds from a diverse pepper patch won't guarantee you will grow a pepper plant true to the mother plant so not a good Idea if you care.  Not also a good Idea if the plant is a hybrid to save any of the seeds because you won't get a true replica to the original plant.You can isolate the plants you want to save seeds from and try to collect seeds but still doesn't mean the pepper flower wasn't pollinated by a flying pollinator moving across your garden or yard.  Odds are low but still could happen.The best solution for true seeds is to bag some flowers right before they bloom and once they bloom hand pollinate and re-bag until the blossoms fall off, and then tag them.  Peppers are self pollinating so you shouldn't have much of a problem.  Now I know for a fact Tomato flowers are only viable for a day or two, but not sure about peppers so hand pollinate as soon as they bloom. I took seeds from a heirloom open pollinated Beaver dam plant packed in a patch with a dozen other types of pepper plants many years ago and grew them.  they weren't  anything like the original, the shape and size was right but flavor wasn't even close and rather nasty.", "images": []}, "Comment 3": {"author_id": "docmommich", "author_name": "docmommich", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/docmommich", "date": "2023-02-25", "text": "Thank you both. You have confirmed my previous beliefs. I know all about isolation techniques, etc. I was just surprised that the need for those techniques was not mentioned up front in these articles about saving seeds. I just read another one, and it did eventually discuss isolation, but not before I'm sure many readers would have long go stopped reading and assumed they could collect seeds from any old pepper. They had even discussed trading seeds with other gardeners, but had not yet mentioned cross pollination, or even hybrids. I worry for folks involved in seed trades, who are hoping for reproduceable varieties. I will redouble my efforts to ensure any seeds I save are as pure as I can make them. Martha", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-154468165", "author_name": "HU-154468165", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-154468165", "date": "2023-02-26", "text": "I've had a succulent plant for years. For the last 6-7 years I've been pruning it to look like a little tree (24 inch long straight stem with a big bushy ball of leaves at the top). But it was getting too top heavy for the 1.5 inch thick stem so I decided to cut the top off and repot it. The repotted top is doing great, but I really wanted the stem to send out new shoots and keep growing in some way. It did send out new shoots just below where I cut it but then it also started to rot from where I cut it. After a few weeks I cut it again below the rot but it eventually rotted again. I tried cutting it below the rot again and putting a turmeric paste over the wound to help it heal but that didn't help- it's still rotting. There's a little bit of growth at the very bottom of the stem (a few inches above the soil) so I know it still has life in it, I'm just worried it's going to rot all the way down to the base. Anyway to get a new cut to scar over so the new growth can keep growing?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "ken-adrian", "author_name": "ken_adrian Adrian MI cold Z5", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ken-adrian", "date": "2023-02-27", "text": "how about some pix ... dont overwater a plant that has no leaves ... especially a jade plant.. explain your system ... ken", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2023-02-27", "text": "It's probably too late, but when you truncate succulents, you can wipe the sap off the wound with a paper towel or clean rag until it stops flowing, then carefully paint the wound with waterproof wood glue. It might not be rot that you're seeing. Wounds in very fleshy plants like Crassula an Aeonium tend to desiccate/ dry out for a considerable proximal distance from the cut. The propagule (or cutting) is usually nowhere near as susceptible to drying out as the rooted portion of the plant; this because the plant is still working to move water upward through the plant's plumbing/ vasculature. I typically save tag ends (the part you cut off after securing) of different size zip ties to use as sort of a spatula. I squeeze the waterproof wood glue onto the zip tie tail. then spread it over the wound carefully, so the wound itself is covered but clue isn't smeared all over the stem below the wound. Typically, that's where you want your back-budding to occur, instead of looking at a bunch of dead/ desiccated tissue. All of these plants are grown from single stems and all were treated with waterproof wood glue as a matter of course. I always treat Crassula and Portulacaria that way, too, along with all wounds larger than about 1/4\" on my bonsai trees as well.    This one ^^^ has been reduced over time and is growing in a Chapstick cap  While I agree with the idea that treating wounds of most trees in the landscape more often than not exacerbates rot issues further down the road, creating problem/ hazardous trees, that doesn't apply to trees grown in containers because they are not subjected to the massive forces of strong wind and tons of weight. title: Cutting back azaleas | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-849091946", "author_name": "HU-849091946", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-849091946", "date": "2023-02-26", "text": "I have Azaleas that are 5 foot tall only green and flower is on the vert tops. They are long stem/trunks with nothing evry ugly except when in blum or have green on ONLY tops.. i would like a fuller more dense bush look.. How far can i cut bacl these bushes?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "luis-pr", "author_name": "luis_pr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/luis-pr", "date": "2023-03-03", "text": "Pruning is seldom needed except for removal of faded flowers (which is called deadheading), but if  you do prune, it is best to prune around March in the Pennsylvania area, understanding that they currently have dormant, spring 2023 flower buds so you may lose all or many spring blooms. Try to limit the number of branches cut to about 1/3 of branches with flower buds. This reduces the spring blooms but the remaining branches will provide some blooms. Typically, there is little need for pruning azaleas and rhododendrons if planted where they can attain their plant label's estimated size at maturity. If growth becomes excessive, reduce the size with light  pruning. Plant form can be improved by pinching out the soft, new shoots in spring. Each spring, after the flower buds start to swell and the smaller leaf  buds become different/obvious, use pinching on the top of the plant  to prevent it from getting taller. Prune out any dead, diseased, crossing, leafless (leafless after the spring leaf out!) or damaged branches, and if the plants have become scraggly, start cutting the oldest  branches back to encourage growth in younger branches. Review throughout the growing season if the sides are not getting much direct sunlight. Where to prune exactly: With larger leaf rhododendrons (elepidotes), only prune just above the growth joints. Each year as the plant starts to grow there is a visible growth joint that indicates where the branch started growth and that is where dormant growth buds are located. With your  azaleas and any small leaf rhododendrons (lepidotes), you can prune anywhere along the branch as the azalea branches have dormant growth buds nearly everywhere.", "images": []}}

title: Cherry tomatoes started indoors | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jeanfrancois-ouellette35", "author_name": "Jean-Francois Ouellette", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jeanfrancois-ouellette35", "date": "2023-02-26", "text": "Hello, A few months ago I planted 3 different cherry tomato plants from my own succesful outdoor seeds in my Aerogarden aeroponics indoor garden. They have grown very tall  even  I I trimmed them regularly so I transplanted them to three 1 liter Mason jar Kratky setups near the windows and they keep growing and I keep trimming them. My question is:  They never flowered. Even if I shook them once in a while to simulate polinating. Is it worth keeping them and transplanting them in my garden in the spring?  Once outside, with the bees, sun and wind, will they start producing fruits???", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "webuser-43509494", "author_name": "Kimberly Wendt (Florida Z. 10b)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-43509494", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "I have two Aero gardens - and I don't usually grow tomatoes or tomato seedlings in them. I'll use peat pots under strong grow lights to do tomatoes. Then when they are about 8\" tall or so, I'll harden them off. 2 weeks later I'll plant outside in containers or huge grow bags. I'll sink the plant down so that 1/2 of it is buried along with roots. Then wait. I usually have rows of 12' tall, crazy prolific tomatoes and lots of fruit. Oh, and I ONLY grow cherry tomatoes. However, for the first time, I tried a micro cherry tomato called Tip Top (something like that). Stays very small and bushy, loads of small orange fruit. Supposedly for growing indoors on window sills or AG type gardens. I've found this actually works in the Aero Garden - but I've had to only grow one or at most, 2 plants (and nothing else) in the AGs. My AGs are all 6 or 7 pod, tall sized.) The tomatoes get sprawling and bushy, and take a good long time to grow. I actually added grow lights in addition to the light on the AG. (FYI, AG lights are replaceable, and you are supposed to replace the after so many hours.) I get a handful of ripe tomatoes about every 3 days or so now. Of course, I get BOWLS full from my outside cherry tomato plants right now... lol. Back to the original OP's questions: Worth saving? Likely. Tomatoes are super adaptable and forgiving. Stop trimming them tho. Up pot them into some 12-14\" diameter and at least 12\" deep pots while you wait for spring to plant them outside. Plant them deeply, sinking the stem at least a couple inches down. That will encourage the stem to grow more roots to support the plant better. In the larger pot, you can add a small cage or trellis to let them grow taller and bushier. They need more light for sure. Get some cheap 'stick in the pot' led grow lights, and add a few to each pot. You'll need to rig up an extension cord/power strip of course. I suggest to stop snipping them because when you do that, you truncate all the growth on that part of the plant for good. You can still have suckers that will overtake the world, but you've truncated the plants natural growth process by trimming them. You'll also need to feed them a bit more often but LESS to keep them happy while they wait. Choose a tomato version fertilizer, that you can dilute into the water to 1/2 strength. Key is to feed more often, but only at 1/2 strength while they are potted. As someone already said, 'shaking' the to induce pollination when there are no flowers is useless. Must have flowers first. Shaking stresses the plant too much, and tomato stalks are notoriously 'snappy'. #1: Don't plant seeds so early. You'll get plants way ahead of nature's timeline in your climate. Look up the info on the tomato variety and read about it's seed germination times. You can plan better next time with that info. #2: if you 'must' pollinate something - simply use a small, soft hair brush to swipe/wipe the flower parts in the order needed. (not foam, not stiff, not a paint brush). Try a makeup brush if you don't have a watercolor brush. You can Google how to do this for your plant (it is different for each type of plant). tldr: Yes. Repot to a much much bigger pot, plant seedling DEEP, set them on the floor, add lots of led grow lights, a trellis or tomato cage, feed 1/2 strength every 2 weeks. Stop pruning, only pinch off suckers in between joints. When spring comes 'harden them off': move them outside during the day, bring inside at night. Do this for at least a week. Then plant. Hope some of this helps you.", "images": []}}

title: Do an addition or update current footprint? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-860381722", "author_name": "HU-860381722", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-860381722", "date": "2023-02-26", "text": "We are trying to decide how best to spend our renovation money.  We have two elementary age children and right now our house is tight, but everyone has their own bedroom and two full bathrooms (no master bathroom).  We only have a small living room with a tv, no family room or basement, but we do use the small bedroom on the first floor as a tv den it and it has a pull out couch for when guests stay. My question is: one project idea is to add an addition on to the back of the house that would give us the dream kitchen with an island, a family room open to the kitchen, and build an unfinished basement that maybe one day we'd have the money to finish off.  The problem with this plan is that it is a real financial reach for us right now, and we would most likely never have the money to do the other projects we want to do in the house (build a master bathroom, fix up the front of our house, and extend over the garage to make the bedrooms more equal and the attic space full height for storage). Plan B is more in-budget, but would not do the addition or the basement.  It would just re-work the footprint of our small kitchen to make it more updated and functional, add a front porch with entrance vestibule with coat closet and bench (like a mudroom), extend over the garage upstairs so both children's rooms were equal, and add a master bathroom.  So overall it would be a nicer, more attractive house, but without that added hang-out space of a basement, bigger kitchen, and family room.  This plan with the smaller kitchen would only seat 2 at the peninsula, so to eat as a family of 4, we could only eat in the dining room, which is a separate room maybe 15 feet away from the kitchen.  I worry about their friends not wanting to come hang out here when they are teens, I like the idea of keeping an eye out and knowing where my children are at those critical ages.  I mean, we do have a small living room with a tv, and then that small den with a tv, but it's hard to compete with the McMansion's all their friends live in.  To be honest, I prefer a small house, but I don't want them to feel \"less than.\"  It's such a small amount of time you need that extra space, it's hard to justify living through all that construction, expense, and added taxes, though the result would be lovely! We love our neighborhood and have looked for other houses for years to see if anything met our needs, but inventory has been terrible. Which plan would you do, and why?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kandrewspa", "author_name": "kandrewspa", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kandrewspa", "date": "2023-02-26", "text": "If you decide to put on an addition, make sure you're not overimproving for your neighborhood.  If you do, you'll never get that money back. I know inventory is low, but what you're talking about is a pretty major expenditure and would be very disruptive.  I would get on the radar of a real estate agent, get preapproved for a loan and be ready to pounce if the right thing comes on the market.  If you have saved enough for a major remodel you are in a good position to make a good offer with a substantial downpayment. On the other hand, if you do nothing, in ten years (?) the kids will leave home and then you'll be happy again that you have a smaller house.  It is good to be able to keep an eye on what the kids are up to no matter what their age.  Remember that there can be all kinds of disfunction going on in those big, beautiful homes.  What's important is that you care and are present for them while they grow up.  While there will no doubt be a period during which they don't appreciate that, it's still something that pays off long-term.  :-)", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "brian130", "author_name": "Brian Kay", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brian130", "date": "2023-02-27", "text": "I'm looking for some feedback and inspiration on a potential kitchen remodel / update and am at the very, very early stages of beginning to think through it. These images are from when we bought the house and basically take you in a circle around the kitchen. We have since replaced the fridge and the oven, both to more modern stainless appliances. We aren't looking for a massive overhaul, we just don't want to invest that much time, energy, and money into it beyond a facelift and a little demo. Our most pressing concern is the counters, and it's two-fold. One, we HATE the tile and grout. Two - we hate the two-tier bar area. It doesn't function well as somewhere to eat all while making drastically reducing useable counter space. Removing it all to one level would also open the space up. Beyond that, we'd replace the sink, drop in a new 30\" cooktop, a new hood, and a new backsplash all around (maybe with something solid behind the cooktop for easier cleanup). I'd love a 36\" cooktop for additional space, but don't have the width needed for the hood and I don't know how the needed space could easily be added. That is what we envision as a first phase. Later, we'd likely paint the walls and refinish/paint the cabinets. But as I said, our biggest priority is getting more usable space and getting rid of the tile and grout. Any thoughts or feedback or considerations to keep in mind (or that we may be overlooking) on this, mostly with phase one? Anything you would do, or wouldn't do? Any thoughts specifically on chopping off the bar and making it all one counter-height level? We don't yet have a material in mind, but we're looking for something durable, low maintenance, and cost effective. We don't need expensive granite or quartz and are fine with more budget-friendly alternatives as long as they are durable, don't need regular maintenance, and of course that they look good. title: When would I expect buds on panicle hydrangea Strawberry Vanilla? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "estherb2", "author_name": "Esther-B, Zone 7a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/estherb2", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "My roses are budding leaves, my dwarf spirea Candy Corn and dwarf weigela My Monet (purple) are budding leaves, but not my other dwarf spirea, dwarf crape myrtles, or Strawberry Vanilla hydrangea. This is my first experience with these, so I'm not sure when to expect leaf buds. We've had a very mild winter this year.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "luis-pr", "author_name": "luis_pr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/luis-pr", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "They are breaking dormancy early. Hydrangea Vanilla Strawberry (VS) is a mid-season hydrangea paniculata summer bloomer. Paniculatas like it begin to develop flower buds depending on their geographical location, weather, etc. but you could say the invisible buds start in late spring or early summer and blooms start soon afterwards so June-July. Here in Texas, VS leafs out in March and blooms in June (it should leaf out later up north though). Crape Myrtles are notoriously very late to leaf out here in Dallas, somewhere between April to May in some years. CMs are currently asleep. Roses here tend to stay evergreen in most years albeit with fewer old leaves by this time and with some leaf out in Feb-March. Spireas are quite hardy, almost impossible to winter kill here. Mine are still dormant in Texas. But sometimes a mild winter with a surprise cold ending is worse than a cold snowy winter. In Atlanta, this happened several decades ago and a large percentage of trees got killed. Periodically check the 10-15 days weather forecasts. Depending on exactly how warm things are, consider mulching, covering with sheets and deeply watering the early risers before any overnight crash in temperatures that might be followed with cold drying winds. Winter has been unusually warm here too; already hit 90F a week ago. Leafing out over here are roses, irises, salvias, azaleas, forsythias, some hydrangeas and a few trees. title: Make-up air for high power range hood in old San Francisco house? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "ashwin-gokhale", "author_name": "Inevitable Remodeler", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/ashwin-gokhale", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "We are in the process of designing our kitchen remodel, and are planning on getting a 36\" six-burner range. Given the aggregate 103,000 BTUs, we are looking at a 42\" wide hood with a 1000 CFM blower. I was feeling good about all of this until I started going down the rabbit hole of make-up air requirements.  My understanding is that you need this under the international building code that many cities have adopted once you have  a 400 CFM+ hood  in order to address potential depressurization and backdraft issues. Based on what I am reading, installing such a system seems potentially overkill in our context and likely to introduce new problems with respect to indoor temperature, cost and maintenance. Our house is 3000 sq feet over three floors with many windows and is built in 1904, so I am sure is far from airtight to begin with. The kitchen is in the center-left of the middle floor and has entrances onleading to the foyer and dining room on two sides and is open to a family room on a third side, so (while not particularly large) is not a closed off room. The family room and dining room have two operable windows and a sliding patio door between them, while the foyer is fully open to a living room with a large bay window. The gas furnace and gas water heater are on the ground floor in the garage which has poor insulation and weather stripping and is far colder at night than the rest of the house.  The gas dryer is in a windowless room on the ground floor with admittedly no ventilation outside of the dryer vent. The house is in San Francisco. Does anyone know if inspectors here actually care about this makeup air system concept in this kind of situation? Apart from what inspectors care about, is this something I need to care about in terms of indoor air quality and safety (we have small kids)?  Thanks in advance from any education anyone is able to provide me on this. I am really grateful for the feedback I have received from others on other aspects of this project so far.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "artemis78", "author_name": "artemis78", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/artemis78", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "Same experience as lharpie--across the bay, and though we did our reno years ago, the requirement was on the books then too. Our city did not care or ask about the MUA for a 700 CFM hood, and we opted not to worry about it because our 1915 home is far from airtight. On the rare occasions when we run the hood on high for more than a few minutes, we do open the back door to draw in more air. (Our kitchen isn't heated to begin with so outdoor air temps aren't generally an issue, except of course for the past few days!) Functionally that's been fine over the years, and we are planning to switch to induction in the next year or so anyway. That said--I would probably consider it for a 1000+ CFM hood, especially if you do at some point plan to replace windows for a more airtight house and intend to stick with gas long-term.", "images": []}}

title: Adding Sliding Door to Open Study Dilemma | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "scott-warren59", "author_name": "Scott Warren", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/scott-warren59", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "I work in the TV and Film space as an editor and I recently moved into a new house with an open study that I use for my work each day. I didn't think it would be such an issue but the noise from people, kids, dogs, and random disruptions is KILLING ME. I'm not entirely sure adding a wall with a door(s) is what I really want to get into, so I was thinking a sliding door could be a path of least resistance. However, I believe there to be some design challenges to this. Design Challenge: There is very little room on the left and right side of the opening to work with. If you're on the outside of the study looking into the space, there is only 9.5\" of space on the left and right side. When standing in the study and looking out, there is a little bit more room to work with 13.5\" on the left side and 24.75\" on the right (but has the light switch on this side). The opening of the study is 8ft. After doing some digging and research, it appears that bipass doors seem to be the best option, and mounting it on the inside of the study. I'm not sure though. I don't know anything about this type of thing, which is why I am posting here. I'd love to hear some suggestions, tips, and alternative solutions! Images of the study are attached for reference.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/3582bd8703fe17ec_6659-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/1972978103fe17f0_6659-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Healthy lifestyle - do you love it or force yourself? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "3katz4me", "author_name": "3katz4me", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3katz4me", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "I was thinking about this yesterday as I cycle in and out of exercise routine enthusiasm.  In the dead of winter in MN, when every outdoor surface is an ice slick, I'm relegated to indoor stuff.  I don't like exercise that's just for the sake of exercise vs some kind of strenuous, productive activity - like yardwork for example.  Unfortunately as an above knee amputee more fun types of exercise (cross country skiing, skating, tennis) aren't feasible though I do hit the tennis ball but can't run across the court so don't really play. (I am going to try pickleball though). I make myself exercise because I know I should if I want to remain alive and active as long as possible but I do not enjoy it.  DH on the other hand seems to genuinely like it and never misses a day. Along the same lines, I will readily admit to enjoying some junk food from time to time - french fries and potato chips for example.  For the most part I like lighter foods - veggies, fish, poultry, nothing rich/creamy or breaded and deep fried - but I don't go out of my way to avoid carbs like pasta, rice, etc. and I'll occasionally have a good burger or steak. I've had an open bag of quinoa in my cupboard for months and finally made something with it this weekend.  I used to use couscous and I think I'm now convinced I'll use quinoa instead going forward.  Fortunately my appetite seems to match my level of activity so I'm not overweight. Anyway, as I was pondering my not overly healthy lifestyle I wondered what others are like - enthusiastically \"all in\" on health and fitness or \"all in\" on enjoying life regardless of how unhealthy it may be or somewhere in the middle.", "images": []}

title: Penne With Vodka Sauce | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "chloebud", "author_name": "chloebud", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chloebud", "date": "2023-02-28", "text": "Making this tonight.  I found the recipe some years ago in one of Ina G\u2019s books.  Simple like most but takes a little longer due to the oven time (also ups the flavor IMO).  A few tweaks\u2026I use a 350 oven and often add sauteed mushrooms to the finished sauce.  I\u2018ve subbed fresh basil for the fresh oregano, too. Penne Alla Vecchia Bettola Serves 4 1/4 cup olive oil2-1/2 cups chopped onion (1 large onion)1 tablespoon minced garlic (3 cloves)1/2 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes (or to taste)1-1/2 teaspoons dried oregano (or to taste)1 cup vodka2 (28-ounce) cans whole peeled plum tomatoes, drainedKosher salt and freshly ground black pepper3/4 pound penne2 tablespoons chopped fresh oregano leaves, plus extra for serving1 cup heavy cream1/2 cup freshly grated Parmesan cheese, plus extra for serving Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Heat the oil in a large (12-inch) ovenproof saut\u00e9 pan over medium heat. Add the onions and garlic and cook for about 5 minutes, until the onions are translucent. Add the red pepper flakes and dried oregano and cook for 1 more minute. Add the vodka and simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, until the mixture is reduced by half. Using clean hands, crush each tomato into the pan. Add 2 teaspoons of salt and 1/2 teaspoon of black pepper. Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid, place in the oven, and bake for 1-1/2 hours. Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add 2 tablespoons of salt and the pasta and cook according to the directions on the package. Drain and set aside. Two cups at a time, carefully pour the tomato mixture into a blender and pur\u00e9e until smooth. Return the tomato mixture to the saut\u00e9 pan (be careful; the handle is hot!). Add the fresh oregano, cream, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper and simmer partially covered for 10 minutes. Add the pasta to the sauce and cook for 2 more minutes. Stir in 1/2 cup of the Parmesan cheese and serve hot sprinkle with extra Parmesan and fresh oregano.", "images": []}
